handoff.purpose: Define frozen dataclasses for type declarations, field declarations, parameter declarations, signature declarations, alias imports, and aggregate type facts.

symbols.name: TypeDecl
symbols.note: Frozen dataclass representing a type declaration (class, dataclass, TypedDict, NamedTuple, Enum, protocol, alias). Fields: name, kind, line, end_line, bases, decorators, alias_target, language.

symbols.name: FieldDecl
symbols.note: Frozen dataclass representing one member of a type. Fields: module, owner, name, line, annotation, origin, has_default, language. origin can be 'annassign', 'assign', 'self', 'enum_member'.

symbols.name: ParamDecl
symbols.note: Frozen dataclass representing one parameter. Fields: name, position, annotation, kind, has_default. kind is 'posonly', 'arg', 'vararg', 'kwonly', 'kwarg'.

symbols.name: SignatureDecl
symbols.note: Frozen dataclass representing a function's surface. Fields: module, qualname, name, line, end_line, owner, params, returns, receiver, is_async, decorators, language.

symbols.name: AliasImport
symbols.note: Frozen dataclass representing a name binding from an import statement. Fields: local, kind, level, module, orig, line.

symbols.name: PyTypeFacts
symbols.note: Frozen dataclass holding raw type facts from one Python file. Fields: module, types, plus others not shown in this chunk? Actually only module and types shown; docstring says 'Every field is a tuple' but only two fields are defined in this chunk.

claims.text: ``origin`` says HOW it was written, because the four ways do not carry the same evidence: ``annassign``, ``assign``, ``self``, ``enum_member``.
claims.why: The docstring describes four origins and the code defines origin with default 'annassign', consistent with the claim.

claims.text: ``annassign``    ``x: int`` in the class body -- the only origin that always carries an annotation.
claims.why: The claim is a description of origin values; the code defines origin as a string field with default 'annassign'. The annotation field defaults to '' and can be non-empty; the claim is consistent.

claims.text: ``assign``       ``x = 10`` in the class body -- a member with no declared type. ``annotation`` is "".
claims.why: The code defines annotation defaulting to '' and origin defaulting to 'annassign', but origin can be set to 'assign'. The claim is consistent.

claims.text: ``self``         ``self.x = ...`` inside a method -- real state, usually unannotated. ``annotation`` is "" unless it was written ``self.x: int = ...``.
claims.why: The annotation field defaults to ''; the claim describes behavior that can be achieved by setting origin to 'self' and annotation accordingly. Consistent.

claims.text: ``enum_member``  ``FAST = "fast"`` in an ``Enum`` body. Enum members are VALUES, not typed fields: ``annotation`` is ALWAYS "" and a consumer must not emit a member->type edge for them, because there is no type to point at.
claims.why: The code allows origin to be 'enum_member' and annotation defaults to ''. The claim about consumer behavior is not enforced by this dataclass but is consistent with the data model.

claims.text: The same name can appear twice with different origins (``limit: int = 10`` in the body plus ``self.limit = limit`` in ``__init__``). Both are kept: they are two different facts about one member, and deciding which one wins is a whole-repo judgement, not a per-file one.
claims.why: The claim about duplicate names being kept is a design statement about how the parser uses FieldDecl; this chunk does not show the parsing logic that would create multiple FieldDecl instances with the same name.

claims.text: ``position`` is 0-based over the concatenation posonly + args + vararg + kwonly + kwarg, in that order -- which is the order a reader sees in the source, not the order Python stores them in.
claims.why: The claim describes how position values are assigned; this chunk does not contain the code that constructs ParamDecl instances, so the ordering claim cannot be verified.

claims.text: ``receiver`` is the name of the implicit first parameter (``self``/``cls``, or whatever the author called it) when this function is a method and NOT a staticmethod; "" otherwise.
claims.why: The claim describes how receiver is populated; this chunk does not contain the logic that determines whether a function is a method or staticmethod.

claims.text: ``_import_records`` above throws ``ast.alias.asname`` away, so ``from x import Result as R`` is unrecoverable from it and the annotation ``R`` could never be resolved.
claims.why: The claim references _import_records which is not defined in this chunk; cannot verify.

claims.text: This record is emitted SEPARATELY rather than by widening that 4-tuple, because the 4-tuple is unpacked positionally in ``resolve_python_imports`` and round-tripped through the disk cache.
claims.why: The claim references resolve_python_imports and a 4-tuple not present in this chunk.

claims.text: A star import is recorded with ``local == "*"`` and ``orig == "*"``: it binds names this file's text does not mention, which is exactly the evidence a resolver needs in order to REFUSE (two star imports from two modules that both declare ``Result`` make ``Result`` ambiguous, and the ambiguity is not visible anywhere else).
claims.why: The claim describes usage of AliasImport in a resolver; not verifiable from this chunk alone.

claims.text: Same contract as ``_import_records``: per-file, expensive, parallelizable work stays here; whole-repo, cheap, serial resolution stays in the parent.
claims.why: References _import_records and a parent resolution layer not present in this chunk.

claims.text: Every field is a tuple, so an instance is immutable and safe as a plain dataclass default on ``FileAnalysis`` (no ``default_factory`` needed) and safe to hand across a process boundary.
claims.why: The claim says 'Every field is a tuple', but in this chunk only two fields are shown: module (str) and types (tuple of TypeDecl). module is not a tuple; it's a str. The claim is false for module.

claims.text: ``truncated`` is True only if the statement descent hit its depth guard, i.e. the file is more deeply nested than any real code -- reported rather than hidden, so a missing type is never silently a missing type.
